courses.title: Hard Floor Care
courses.description:
Hard Floor Care is a blended course for technicians, supervisors and facility cleaners in Australia and New Zealand who clean, restore and maintain tile, stone, resilient and timber floors. The online part builds the judgement to decide before acting: which floor and surface layer is in front of you, what the label, the safety data sheet and the maker’s instructions allow, and when to stop. A supervised practical day then assesses the skills on real samples.

Six modules cover the three floor families and the pre-job check, including the asbestos question (identify, presume, stop and refer, with no work method taught for suspected asbestos); identifying the floor and choosing chemistry by compatibility; machines and the approved setup record; tile, stone and grout; resilient and coated timber floors; and quoting, handover and records. Every lesson has a worked metric example, a diagram, a field tool and a sources list. Power maths use 230 V and a 10 A outlet as the worked example.

No universal pH band, pad colour, machine speed or pressure is taught. The method is to read the product and maker’s instructions, record the approved setup, test, and stop if limits cannot be established. It does not replace a manufacturer’s instructions, a Safety Data Sheet or a site’s own rules. Australian and New Zealand practice are stated side by side where they differ.

This course is not an IICRC or ATFA certification and carries no continuing education credit. Any credential is CARSI-issued only after the practical sign-off.
courses.shortDescription: A blended course for Australia and New Zealand: the three hard floor families, the asbestos stop-and-refer gate, floor identification, chemistry by compatibility, machines and the approved setup record, tile and grout, resilient and timber floors, quoting and handover, then a supervised practical day.

modules.title: Module 1: Safe Start and the Three Floor Families

lessons.title: Three floor families and the surface layer
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A cafe owner in Newtown, Sydney, asks for a deep clean of 62 m² of mixed flooring: glazed tiles in the kitchen, sheet vinyl in the dining area and a spotted gum strip at the entry. The last contractor used one strong cleaner on all three. The vinyl is dull, the timber has white patches and the owner wants it fixed before Friday. Nobody wrote down what each floor was.

The idea

Every hard floor belongs to one of three families, and each family fails in its own way. Tile and stone covers glazed ceramic, porcelain, quarry tile and terracotta, and natural stone such as marble, limestone, travertine, granite and slate. Resilient covers sheet vinyl, vinyl tile, luxury vinyl plank and tile, linoleum and rubber. Timber covers solid and engineered boards with a coating on top. This grouping is a CARSI teaching device. No regulator or standard defines it, and it exists only to sort the ways a floor gets damaged.

One idea carries the whole course: most of the time you are cleaning a surface layer, not the floor. That layer may be the glaze on a tile, the factory finish on vinyl or linoleum, a polish applied on site, or the coating on a timber floor. Keep the surface layer healthy and the floor lasts. Damage it and the floor looks old long before it is worn out.

Each family has a typical way of failing. Calcium-based stone such as marble and limestone is etched by acids. A stone supplier’s Australian care guide states that acidic products can etch calcium-based stones like marble and limestone, and etching is a change to the stone itself, not a stain that cleans off. Timber suffers when water and heat get into the boards and under the coating. The Australasian Timber Flooring Association (ATFA) advises that, unless the timber flooring or finish manufacturer says it is acceptable, it is safest to assume steam cleaning is not appropriate on a timber floor. Resilient floors are decided by the maker’s care sheet: one commercial sheet vinyl guide from Godfrey Hirst says to dilute chemicals to appropriate levels for each application, following the cleaner’s instructions.

That is the pattern for the whole course. The family tells you what to worry about, but it does not tell you what to do. The floor in front of you does, and so do the label, the safety data sheet (SDS) and the maker’s instructions for that product. A pack of “rules” such as one pH band, one pad colour or one machine speed for a whole family is exactly how the cafe floors above were damaged. The method is to identify the floor and its coating, read the label, the SDS and the manufacturer’s instructions, record the approved setup, test in a hidden spot, and stop if the limits cannot be established.

Two checks come before any of that, and the next lessons cover both: the asbestos question, and the rest of the pre-job check (SDS, protective equipment, slip risk and power). Nothing in this course is a licence to start work before those are done.

See it

The three CARSI floor families. The family points to the risk. The label, SDS and maker’s instructions decide the method.

Do it in metric

Size the cafe before anything else. The kitchen is 4.2 m × 3.5 m = 14.7 m². The dining area is 6.1 m × 5.2 m = 31.7 m². The entry strip is 2.6 m × 6.0 m = 15.6 m². Together that is 14.7 + 31.7 + 15.6 = 62.0 m².

Now sort them: the kitchen is tile and stone, the dining area is resilient and the entry strip is timber. Three families means three job-sheet lines, three sets of label and SDS checks and three sets of hidden-spot tests, not one product at one dilution across 62.0 m². The same number of square metres can need three different plans.

Field download

The Floor family and surface layer card lists the three families, the typical way each fails and the three questions to answer before any product is opened. Print it and keep it on the clipboard.

Check yourself

The Module 1 check asks you to sort floors into families, name what damages each family and say why a family label alone is not enough to choose a method.

Takeaway

Sort the floor into a family, then identify the surface layer you are about to clean. The family warns you; the label, SDS and maker’s instructions decide. Next: the asbestos question.

Sources for this lesson

  • Australian stone supplier guide, How to clean natural stone without damaging it. Read 16/11/2026.
  • Australasian Timber Flooring Association, Floor care and maintenance (2016, hosted by Resene). Read 16/11/2026.
  • Godfrey Hirst, Maintenance Recommendations for Commercial Sheet Vinyl, Australia / New Zealand (August 2022). Read 16/11/2026.

lessons.title: Asbestos: identify, presume, stop and refer
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A property manager in Brisbane books a restorative clean and recoat of the vinyl tile floor in a 1996 community hall. The tiles are lifting at one doorway and the manager says the floor has always been fine. There is no asbestos register on file and the original fit-out records have gone. The crew arrives with a rotary machine and a stripper already mixed in the van.

The idea

Asbestos is the first check on any older floor, because it changes everything that follows. Australia totally banned asbestos from 31 December 2003, but the ban did not remove asbestos already installed. In New Zealand, WorkSafe says any building built or renovated before 2000 could contain asbestos, and lists floor tiles and vinyl sheeting among the products that used it. The national model code in Australia notes that bathrooms, toilets and laundries may have asbestos sheeting or vinyl tiles.

You cannot tell by looking. A NSW Government page states that you can’t tell if building materials contain asbestos just by looking at them, and WorkSafe New Zealand notes that fibres are too small to be seen. So the course teaches a decision, not a visual test: identify, presume, stop, refer.

Identify. Ask when the floor was laid and whether the floor and any adhesive have been tested. Ask whether an asbestos register or report exists, and record the answer. Presume. Under the national model code, a person with management or control of a workplace must assume material is asbestos if it cannot be identified but a competent person reasonably believes it is. Assumed asbestos is treated as asbestos for legal purposes, and the suspect material can stay undisturbed without sampling. For a cleaning crew the working version is plain: if a floor laid before the ban cannot be shown to be asbestos-free, treat it as suspected asbestos-containing material.

Stop and refer. If asbestos is suspected or cannot be ruled out, stop the exercise and refer the proposed work for competent, jurisdiction-specific assessment. This course does not authorise stripping, abrasion, machine treatment or removal of suspected asbestos-containing material, and it gives no method for working on it. That is deliberate: the instruction is a hold, not a technique. Work does not resume until a competent person has confirmed in writing what is permitted and what controls apply. Broken, lifting or crumbling tiles raise the stakes further: stop, keep people out and report it.

Law matters here. WorkSafe New Zealand explains that its Asbestos Regulations generally prohibit work involving asbestos, with listed exceptions such as removal and sampling, and that some tasks can only be done by licensed businesses. State and territory rules in Australia differ on assessment, registers and licensing. The licence classes and area limits are not taught in this draft and are flagged for a qualified reviewer. Removal of asbestos-containing material is licensed work. It is never part of a cleaning job.

See it

The asbestos gate. The answer to any doubt is to stop and refer, not to choose a gentler method.

Do it in metric

The hall floor measures 6.5 m × 5.8 m = 37.7 m². That whole area becomes a stopped area until a competent person confirms in writing what is permitted. Mark the doorway where tiles are lifting on the sketch and keep people and trolleys out of that 37.7 m².

Write the decision on the job sheet in three lines: floor laid 1996, before the 31 December 2003 ban; no register or test result sighted; decision: suspected asbestos-containing material, stop and refer. The date, the person told and the time go beside it. Numbers do not clear a floor. A date that falls after the ban lowers the risk, but only a competent assessment settles it.

Field download

The Pre-job check and stop sheet puts the asbestos questions first, then the SDS, protective equipment, slip and power checks, and ends with a go or stop decision and who was told.

Check yourself

The Module 1 check asks you to apply the Australian and New Zealand dates, to say what to do when a floor cannot be shown to be asbestos-free and to choose stop and refer over a gentler method.

Takeaway

If asbestos cannot be ruled out, stop and refer. No date, colour or tile pattern clears a floor, and this course teaches no method for suspected asbestos. Next: the other checks that come before work starts.

Sources for this lesson

  • NSW Government, When was asbestos banned in Australia?. Read 16/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe New Zealand, Asbestos in Aotearoa New Zealand. Read 16/11/2026.
  • Safe Work Australia, Model Code of Practice: How to manage and control asbestos in the workplace. Read 16/11/2026.

lessons.title: SDS, protective equipment, slip risk and power
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A crew in Geelong arrives to machine-scrub a school corridor. The cleaner’s SDS is not on site, the only power point is shared with the staff room, and a student walks across the wet patch because the sign is leaning against the wall. A teacher asks how long it will take and whether the product is safe around children.

The idea

The pre-job check is the one part of the course you cannot fail. Before any chemical or machine touches a floor, four things must be true: you hold the SDS for every product, you have chosen the controls from the top of the hierarchy down, you have dealt with slip risk, and the power is safe.

Duty and controls. In Australia, a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU) has a primary duty of care for the health and safety of workers and others affected by the work. In New Zealand, section 36 of the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 sets out the same duty of care, so far as is reasonably practicable. Safe Work Australia says to aim to eliminate risks first, and, if that is not possible, to minimise them so far as is reasonably practicable. Safe Work Australia ranks personal protective equipment (PPE) among the least effective controls, so it is not the first control to choose.

The SDS. Anyone who supplies, uses or stores hazardous chemicals must keep copies of the SDS in the workplace. For each product, find four things before you open it: the hazards and any dangerous goods classification, the protective equipment it asks for, the first aid and spill steps, and anything it says about mixing, ventilation or surfaces it must not touch. Mix only at the label dilution, label every bottle and bucket, never mix two products, ventilate and dispose of wastewater to the site’s or council’s rules. In an emergency, ring 000. For poisoning advice, the Poisons Information Centre helpline is available 24/7 on 13 11 26. In New Zealand, the National Poisons Centre is on 0800 764 766 (0800 POISON) and the emergency number is 111.

Slip. Safe Work Australia notes that slips, trips and falls can happen in almost any workplace and can cause serious injuries. A wet hard floor is a fall waiting to happen: signs out before the first pass, a dry walkway, and a barrier where the public can reach. In Australia, wet slip resistance is classified under AS 4586, Slip resistance classification of new pedestrian surface materials. Because a published class describes a new surface, a coating applied later can change how the floor grips. On commercial jobs, note the slip class if one exists, record any test done afterwards and call an accredited slip tester when in doubt.

Power. Australian and New Zealand supply is a nominal 230 V. The worked example uses an outlet figure of 10 A; the circuit’s own rating is a separate figure that must be confirmed on site. Use an RCD (safety switch), inspect leads and plugs before each job, and keep electrical equipment in a current test-and-tag cycle. AS/NZS 3760 sets out the methods for in-service safety inspection and testing of electrical equipment and RCDs; the state regulator and the standard decide how often. Add up the machine currents on each circuit before plugging in, and check the total against that circuit’s rating and everything else already on it. A circuit that trips mid-pass leaves a wet floor and a halted machine.

See it

The four-part pre-job check. A missing SDS, an unsafe circuit or no signs is a stop, not a delay.

Do it in metric

Take one outlet rated 10 A as the example figure. At 230 V it supplies at most 230 × 10 = 2,300 W. The scrubber and wet vacuum for the corridor draw 5.5 A and 4.0 A on their data plates, which is 5.5 + 4.0 = 9.5 A together, or 230 × 9.5 = 2,185 W. That leaves 10 − 9.5 = 0.5 A of the 10 A outlet figure.

Verdict: do not run both machines at once on that outlet. The circuit’s own rating, and everything else already on it (such as the staff room), must be confirmed on site before either power option is chosen: read the breaker at the switchboard, and ask the site contact or an electrician. Then run one machine at a time, or use a separate circuit that has enough capacity. Read the current from each machine’s data plate, because the figures here are only an illustration.

Field download

The same Pre-job check and stop sheet carries the SDS, protective equipment, slip and power checks. Complete it for every job and keep a copy with the job file.

Check yourself

The Module 1 check asks you to name the duty holder, say what must be on site before a product is opened and decide when a power or slip problem is a stop.

Takeaway

SDS on site, controls from the top down, signs out, safe power. If any one is missing, stop and fix it before work starts. Next: Module 2, identifying the floor and its surface layer.

Sources for this lesson

  • Safe Work Australia, Duties of a PCBU. Read 16/11/2026.
  • New Zealand Legislation, Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, section 36. Read 16/11/2026.
  • Safe Work Australia, Manage the risks. Read 16/11/2026.
  • Safe Work Australia, Safety data sheets. Read 16/11/2026.
  • Safe Work Australia, Slips, trips and falls. Read 16/11/2026.
  • NSW Poisons Information Centre, About. Read 16/11/2026.
  • National Poisons Centre (New Zealand), Contact. Read 16/11/2026.
  • New Zealand Police, 111 Emergency Services. Read 16/11/2026.
  • SafeWork NSW, Electrical inspection and testing. Read 16/11/2026.
  • ACO Drain, Understanding slip resistance (secondary summary of AS 4586). Read 16/11/2026.

modules.title: Module 2: Identify the Floor and Choose Chemistry by Compatibility

lessons.title: The floor identification routine
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A strata manager in Perth sends a crew to refresh the lobby floor of a 2008 apartment building. It is a pale, speckled hard floor with a shiny surface. The invoice says “stone tile” and the owners’ committee wants it back to “as new”. Nobody on site can say whether it is marble, limestone or porcelain, or whether anything was ever applied to it.

The idea

Naming the floor and its finish comes before choosing a method. Five minutes of identification prevents most damage claims. The routine has five steps, and the order matters because each step narrows the risk.

1. Look and feel. Is it hard and cold (tile or stone), warm and flexible (resilient) or grained and warm (timber)? Look at seams, edges, grout lines and any threshold strips. These cues are starting points only. They tell you where to look next, not what the floor is.

2. Look for records. Ask the owner or manager for the purchase invoice, the maker’s name, the installer, any care sheet and any warranty. A care sheet from the maker beats any guess. Photograph the floor in place and any markings on offcuts or in cupboards.

3. Stone and tile. If a tile floor is stone, find out which stone. Marble, limestone and travertine are calcium-based and are etched by acidic products, as an Australian stone supplier’s care guide states. That is why a stone you cannot identify is treated as acid-sensitive: use only products the maker states are safe for stone, and obtain advice before anything stronger. Granite and slate are different stones with different problems, such as sealer build-up, but you only treat them as different once they are positively identified. For routine care the same guide recommends warm water, a soft cloth and a pH-neutral cleaner.

4. Resilient and timber. For resilient floors, the type decides which maker’s sheet to read: sheet vinyl, vinyl tile, plank, linoleum and rubber all have different care sheets and some carry a factory finish the maker wants left in place. For timber, find out the coating. The Australasian Timber Flooring Association (ATFA) care sheet lists cleaning options by coating type and tells the reader to follow the advice provided by the coating manufacturer, so a coating you cannot name is a stop.

5. Test a hidden spot, then record. One commercial vinyl maker’s sheet says: if in doubt, test in an inconspicuous area. Use the product and dilution you intend to use, a small area, the dwell the label states, and write down what happened. Then write the floor type, the surface layer and the condition on the job sheet. If you still cannot identify the floor, stop and ask the manufacturer or an expert.

See it

The five-step identification routine. Each step narrows the risk before any product is opened.

Do it in metric

Treat the hidden spot as a measured test. Mark a square 100 mm × 100 mm, which is 0.1 m × 0.1 m = 0.01 m², in a spot nobody will notice, such as under a door or behind a plant. Apply the intended product at the label dilution for the stated dwell, rinse as the label says and write the result in the record.

In a class lab with 12 sample boards, 10 correct identifications is 10 ÷ 12 = 83.3%. Use the lab to see how many floors you named from records rather than appearance. A floor named by appearance alone is a guess.

Field download

The Floor ID and compatibility record holds the five identification steps, the hidden-spot test and the chemistry check from the next lesson on one page.

Check yourself

The Module 2 check asks you to sort identification cues, apply the stone and timber coating rules and decide when to stop.

Takeaway

Identify the floor by records first, appearance second and a small recorded hidden spot third. A stone you cannot name is treated as acid-sensitive. Next: choosing chemistry by compatibility.

Sources for this lesson

  • Australian stone supplier guide, How to clean natural stone without damaging it. Read 16/11/2026.
  • Australasian Timber Flooring Association, Floor care and maintenance (2016, hosted by Resene). Read 16/11/2026.
  • Godfrey Hirst, Maintenance Recommendations for Commercial Sheet Vinyl, Australia / New Zealand (August 2022). Read 16/11/2026.

lessons.title: Chemistry: soil, surface, label and SDS
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A facility cleaner in Adelaide buys a strong degreaser for a food-court floor and uses it on every floor in the centre: porcelain tiles, a polished vinyl walkway and a polished timber feature stair. Within a week the vinyl has lost its gloss and the stair has white marks along the edges. The delivery note named the product but nobody looked at the label or the SDS.

The idea

A common trap in floor care is choosing a product by the name of the soil, or by a rule that one product or one pH suits a whole family. That is how the three floors in the food court were damaged. The method here is different: choose chemistry for both the soil and the identified surface, using the product label, the SDS and the manufacturer’s instructions for the floor.

Start with the floor. Once the floor and its surface layer are identified (Lesson 2.1), find what the floor maker says. For timber, ATFA directs the reader to the coating manufacturer’s advice, and treats steam as unsuitable unless the maker approves it. For resilient floors, a maker’s care sheet states the products and tools that suit that product. For natural stone, an Australian stone supplier advises avoiding vinegar, bleach, abrasive powders and scouring pads on natural stone.

Then the product. The label gives the dilution, the contact time and the surfaces the product is not for. The SDS lists the hazards, the protective equipment, the first aid and spill steps and any incompatibilities. Anyone who uses hazardous chemicals must keep the SDS in the workplace. Never mix two products. Dilute only as the label says: one commercial vinyl maker’s sheet says to always dilute chemicals to appropriate levels for each application, following the cleaner’s instructions.

pH is information, not proof. A pH reading tells you how acidic or alkaline a solution is. It does not tell you whether the product is safe on a given floor, because surface compatibility, formulation, concentration and method also matter. Some makers define a neutral band for their own product, and one commercial sheet vinyl guide defines a neutral cleaner for that product as one reading pH 6 to 8. That figure belongs to that maker’s product. It is an example of a maker setting a limit, not a band for all floors. If a floor maker does not publish a limit, the right move is to ask, not to assume one.

Then test. Make a hidden-spot test with the exact product, dilution and dwell you intend to use, then record the result. If the test shows any change in gloss, colour or surface feel, stop. If the compatibility or the limits cannot be established, stop and obtain technical advice rather than substituting a generic band. This is the same pattern for every product in every module: identify, read, record, test, stop if limits cannot be set.

See it

Choosing chemistry. The floor and the maker come first. The pH figure never replaces the maker’s instructions.

Do it in metric

A label gives a dilution of 1 part product to 20 parts water. One part in 21 total is product, so a 10 L bucket needs 10 ÷ 21 = 0.476 L of product and 10 − 0.476 = 9.524 L of water. Use a marked measuring jug, not a splash from the bottle.

A job needs 12 buckets of 10 L. That is 12 × 0.476 = 5.71 L of product in total. Round up when you buy and record the lot in the job file. If the label’s ratio differs, use the label’s ratio: 1:20 is an illustration only.

Field download

The Floor ID and compatibility record also holds the chemistry check: label, SDS, maker’s instructions, dilution, hidden-spot result and the stop rule.

Check yourself

The Module 2 check asks you to choose chemistry by compatibility, say what a pH reading does and does not prove and calculate a dilution.

Takeaway

Choose chemistry for the soil and the identified surface, from the label, SDS and maker’s instructions. A pH reading alone never proves safety. Next: machines and the approved setup record.

Sources for this lesson

  • Godfrey Hirst, Maintenance Recommendations for Commercial Sheet Vinyl, Australia / New Zealand (August 2022). Read 16/11/2026.
  • Australian stone supplier guide, How to clean natural stone without damaging it. Read 16/11/2026.
  • Safe Work Australia, Safety data sheets. Read 16/11/2026.
  • Australasian Timber Flooring Association, Floor care and maintenance (2016, hosted by Resene). Read 16/11/2026.

modules.title: Module 3: Machines, Tools and the Approved Setup Record

lessons.title: Which machine for which job, and the pre-start check
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A junior technician in a Brisbane shopping centre is told to deal with a dirty corridor before opening. The only machine on the trolley is a single-disc rotary with a stiff pad. The lead has a nicked sheath, the RCD has not been tested and the solution tank still holds yesterday’s mix. The floor is vinyl. Ten minutes later the machine trips the circuit and the floor is wet and unsigned.

The idea

Three kinds of equipment do most hard floor jobs, and the skill is picking the right one for the floor and the job. This lesson describes the job each does. It does not give settings, because settings belong to the maker of the floor, the product and the tool (Lesson 3.2).

Truck-mount with a hard-surface spinner tool. Used on tile, grout, rough stone and concrete for rinse and recovery with hot water. It needs separate truck-mount operating training and a site that can handle the wastewater. This course covers only the choice of the hard-surface tool and the checks around it. Single-disc rotary machine. Used for scrubbing and for coating removal with the pad the approved setup names, always with solution fed to the floor and recovered promptly. Counter-rotating brush and auto scrubber. Used for maintenance scrubs, agitating grout before extraction and low-moisture work on larger areas. One floor maker’s commercial sheet vinyl guide states that auto scrubbing in unobstructed areas takes approximately 20 percent of the time of damp mopping, and that damp mopping should be used in obstructed areas only.

How do you choose? Start with the floor and the surface layer, because they decide what the equipment may do. Then match the job: loosening soil, removing a coating, agitating grout, rinsing and recovering, or maintaining. Then match the area: large and open favours a scrubber, tight and obstructed favours hand tools and a damp mop. Then check the machine can do the job without breaking the limits set in the approved setup. If it cannot, change the machine, not the limit.

Pre-start check, every machine, every job. Leads and plugs undamaged, with no cuts, taped joins or exposed conductors. RCD in use and tested. The test-and-tag date is current. AS/NZS 3760 covers in-service safety inspection and testing of electrical equipment and RCDs, and the state regulator and the standard decide the intervals. Pad driver or brush fitted and secure, and the pad or brush matches the approved setup. Solution tank clean and filled with a fresh, correctly diluted mix. For a truck mount, recovery hose and filters checked and spinner jets clear. Signs out before the first pass: one maker’s sheet says to post wet floor signs and wipe up spillages immediately.

Wear items. A pull-apart session on the practical day shows the parts of each machine and the wear item to check on each: pads and drivers, brushes and cassettes, drive belts, guards and skirts, hoses, jets and filters. Worn items change what the machine does to the floor, so a pass that looked acceptable last month can scratch or leave streaks today.

See it

The three kinds of equipment and the job each does. The approved setup, not the machine, sets the limits.

Do it in metric

A damp-mop pass over 120 m² of open corridor takes the crew 2.0 h on their own timed record. Using the maker’s figure, an auto scrubber needs 20% of that, or 0.2 × 2.0 = 0.4 h, which is 24 min. The saving is 2.0 − 0.4 = 1.6 h, or 96 min.

Check the starting point too: 120 m² ÷ 2.0 h = 60 m²/h by damp mop. Time your own crew before quoting from any maker’s ratio, because the ratio is one maker’s estimate for open areas, not a promise for your site.

Field download

The Machine pre-start and approved setup record carries the pre-start checklist for every machine and the approved setup record from the next lesson.

Check yourself

The Module 3 check asks you to match equipment to a job, work through the pre-start check and say who sets a machine’s limits.

Takeaway

Choose the equipment for the floor and the job, and run the pre-start check before the first pass. The approved setup sets the limits, not the machine. Next: the approved setup record.

Sources for this lesson

  • Godfrey Hirst, Maintenance Recommendations for Commercial Sheet Vinyl, Australia / New Zealand (August 2022). Read 16/11/2026.
  • SafeWork NSW, Electrical inspection and testing. Read 16/11/2026.

lessons.title: The approved setup record
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A contractor in Hobart is asked to restore a school hall floor. The owner wants it done the way the last job was done, with the same pad, the same speed and the same pressure. Nobody knows what the last job was, and the floor maker, the coating and the product are all different. A supervisor asks the crew to write down what they will use and where each setting came from.

The idea

Hard floor damage rarely comes from a bad machine. It comes from a setting copied from a different job. Pad colour, machine speed, pressure and temperature are not rules that carry from floor to floor. They are values a maker sets for a floor, a coating, a product and a tool. The approved setup is the written record of those values for the job in front of you, and where each one came from.

What the record holds. The floor and the surface layer identified in Lesson 2.1. The product and the dilution from the label. The dwell and contact time from the label. The pad or brush, named by what the maker says, and the speed. For a truck-mount tool, the pressure and temperature limits from the maker of the floor, the grout and the tool. Recovery and drying requirements. Where each value came from: the floor maker’s sheet, the product label or SDS, the tool maker’s manual or the technical reviewer. And the hidden-spot test result.

Why not one rule. Pads are specified by the maker for the product. One commercial vinyl guide names a red scrubbing pad or equivalent for light scrubbing and a blue pad for deeper scrubbing, and gives 300 rpm or lower for a wet scrub with a swing machine. That sheet is an example of a maker specifying a setup for its own product. It is not a pad colour or a speed to carry to any other floor. A different floor, coating or product will have a different setup. The same is true of pressure and temperature on a hard-surface tool, and the review pack’s single pressure figure for it is held back for a qualified reviewer.

Where to find it. ATFA says to use the cleaning regime specified by the floor coating manufacturer where possible. The label and SDS state the dilution and the contact time. Floor makers publish care sheets. Tool makers publish manuals. If you cannot find a maker’s value, ask the maker, the supplier or the technical reviewer. If you still cannot establish the limit, stop and obtain technical advice. Do not substitute a generic number.

When to stop. Stop when the floor or coating cannot be identified, when the maker’s limits cannot be found, when a hidden-spot test changes the surface, or when the equipment cannot stay within the limit. Stopping is not failure. It is the control that keeps a floor from becoming a claim.

See it

The approved setup record. Every value has a named source, and a missing limit means stop.

Do it in metric

A 2 m² test patch takes 0.2 L of mixed solution, so the rate is 0.2 ÷ 2 = 0.1 L/m². The hall is 60 m², so it needs 0.1 × 60 = 6 L. Add a 20% allowance for edges and re-treatment: 6 × 1.2 = 7.2 L.

Write the rate and the source on the record: “0.1 L/m² measured on test patch, 2 m², label dwell as stated”. A recorded measurement is a defence. A guess is not.

Field download

The same Machine pre-start and approved setup record has one blank approved setup per task. Fill it in before starting and keep it with the job file.

Check yourself

The Module 3 check asks you to say what an approved setup holds, why a pad colour or speed is not a rule and what to do when a limit cannot be found.

Takeaway

No pressure, pH band, pad colour or speed carries from one floor to the next. Record the maker’s values for this floor, coating, product and tool, test, and stop if limits cannot be established. Next: tile, stone and grout.

Sources for this lesson

  • Godfrey Hirst, Maintenance Recommendations for Commercial Sheet Vinyl, Australia / New Zealand (August 2022). Read 16/11/2026.
  • Australasian Timber Flooring Association, Floor care and maintenance (2016, hosted by Resene). Read 16/11/2026.

lessons.title: Tile and grout restorative clean
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A restaurant owner in Fremantle books a restorative clean of a 20 m² kitchen floor in 300 mm glazed tiles with dark, greasy grout. The last clean used a high-pressure wand, and the grout is now sandy in two places. A cabinet toe-kick has started to swell. The owner wants it done overnight and the kitchen must reopen at 7 am.

The idea

A restorative clean with hot rinse and recovery reaches soil that a mop never does, but it only works on tile and grout that can take it. The sequence below follows the identified floor and the recorded setup (Module 3). It gives no settings, because those come from the makers.

Prepare. Do the pre-job check, identify the floor and complete the approved setup record first. If the floor is stone, check the stone before you choose a product: calcium-based stone takes neutral, stone-safe products only. A stone supplier’s guide advises avoiding vinegar, bleach, abrasive powders and scouring pads on natural stone. Remove dry soil by vacuuming or dust-mopping, as one maker’s guide does before wet work. Protect skirting, carpet edges and cabinetry with tape or film.

Test the grout first. Before any pressure, tap the tiles and scratch the grout in a grid of test points. Loose, crumbling or sandy grout, or tiles that sound hollow or drummy, means stop: the floor is not ready for a restorative clean. Quote a re-grout or remedial work instead. This is the stop rule that protects the owner and the contractor.

Clean. Pre-spray the product at the label dilution and let it dwell for the time on the label, keeping the surface wet as the label directs. Agitate the grout lines with the grout brush or counter-rotating brush named in the approved setup. Then rinse and recover with the tool, overlapping passes, using only the pressure and temperature limits recorded in the approved setup for the identified floor and equipment. Where limits cannot be established, stop and obtain technical advice. Detail the edges with a hand tool, and squeegee pooled water to recovery.

Finish. One maker’s guide for vinyl says to rinse thoroughly with fresh clean water, remove the rinse water and let the floor dry completely. The principle applies here: check the result in raking light, re-treat any problem lines, and dry the floor fully before any grout sealer. If a sealer will go on, check the slip risk as in Lesson 1.3. Wastewater. NSW EPA guidance states that nothing other than clean rainwater should enter the stormwater drain on or near the premises, and that it is against the law to place material where it can flow into a waterway. Confirm the site and council trade-waste route before you start; local rules differ.

See it

The tile and grout sequence. Loose or crumbling grout ends the job before any pressure is used.

Do it in metric

A 300 mm tile covers 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09 m². The 20 m² kitchen holds about 20 ÷ 0.09 = 222 tiles. Each tile adds about 0.6 m of shared grout line, so the floor has roughly 222 × 0.6 = 133 m of grout line to agitate, ignoring the edges.

Plan the tap test as a grid: one test point per m² gives 20 points. Mark them on a sketch and record Pass or Stop at each. One failure in a high-traffic strip is enough to stop and re-quote that strip. Time a 2 m² test panel before you promise a finish time, because the time is a measured number, not a planning figure from a pack.

Field download

The Tile, stone and grout job sheet has the tap-and-scratch grid, the approved setup lines, the re-treatment list and the before and after photo record.

Check yourself

The Module 4 check asks you to order the tile and grout sequence, apply the grout stop rule and name where wastewater must not go.

Takeaway

Test the grout before pressure, follow the recorded setup and dry the floor before sealing. Loose grout means stop and quote remedial work. Next: coatings on tile and stone.

Sources for this lesson

  • Godfrey Hirst, Maintenance Recommendations for Commercial Sheet Vinyl, Australia / New Zealand (August 2022). Read 16/11/2026.
  • Australian stone supplier guide, How to clean natural stone without damaging it. Read 16/11/2026.
  • NSW EPA, Guidance for stormwater management: the drain is just for rain. Read 16/11/2026.

lessons.title: Coatings on tile and stone, sealers and slip
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A body corporate in Melbourne asks a crew to deal with a hazy, slippery foyer floor of cream tiles. A previous contractor applied a shiny coating years ago, and nobody has the product name. One small corner has dull, etched patches near the lift. A resident slipped last week on a wet day and the strata manager now wants a number for slip resistance and a clean.

The idea

Old coatings are the usual reason a tile or stone floor looks hazy, patchy or slippery. The job starts with identifying what is on the floor, because the right method depends on the coating and on the tile or stone underneath it. This lesson teaches the identify, test and record steps. The removal method itself comes from the approved setup and the makers’ instructions.

Identify the coating. Scratch a hidden area with a fingernail, place a water drop on it, and make a hidden-spot test with the product you intend to use, as a maker’s guide says: if in doubt, test in an inconspicuous area or on a sample offcut first. Record what the coating appears to be: a wax, an acrylic sealer, an oil, or unknown. If it is unknown, you do not yet have enough to choose a method.

Know the tile or stone. Glazed tile, porcelain, quarry tile and terracotta behave differently, and so do the natural stones. Calcium-based stone such as marble, limestone and travertine is etched by acidic products, so a stripper or cleaner that is not stone-safe can do permanent damage. Etched patches are not a cleaning problem. An Australian stone supplier advises seeking professional advice for dull or etched patches, which is what the foyer corner needs. Do not apply wax or polish to glazed tile unless the tile maker states it is suitable.

Choose the method from the makers. Both the product label and the tile or stone maker must accept the method. The approved setup states the product, the dilution, the dwell, the tool and the limits. Heavy build-up on stone may need mechanical correction by a specialist, so refer it rather than escalate the chemistry. After removal, rinse, check, dry fully and record the condition before any sealer goes on. Collect rinse water and do not let it reach the stormwater drain: NSW EPA guidance says nothing other than clean rainwater should enter it.

Slip. AS 4586, Slip resistance classification of new pedestrian surface materials, classifies the wet slip resistance of new surfaces. The class describes a new surface, so removing or adding a coating can change how the floor grips. Note the class if one exists before you coat, record any test you or a slip tester carry out afterwards, and call an accredited slip tester when in doubt. A resident who slipped is a reason to test, not to guess.

See it

Coatings on tile and stone. An unknown coating or etched stone ends the job until advice is obtained.

Do it in metric

The foyer corner to be resealed measures 3.5 m × 2.4 m = 8.4 m². A label states a coverage of 8 m² per litre per coat (an illustrative figure). Two coats need 8.4 × 2 ÷ 8 = 2.1 L. Add a 10% allowance for edges and the porous patches: 2.1 × 1.1 = 2.31 L.

Before sealing, record the slip class if you have one and book the test for after the cure. Write the numbers on the job sheet so the strata manager can see what was measured and when.

Field download

The Tile, stone and grout job sheet has a coating test record, the approved setup lines for removal and sealing, and a slip note.

Check yourself

The Module 4 check asks you to identify a coating, say when a stone floor needs professional advice and say what a slip class does and does not describe.

Takeaway

Identify the coating and the tile or stone first, take the method from the makers, dry before sealing and record slip risk. Unknown coating or etched stone means obtain advice. Next: resilient and timber floors.

Sources for this lesson

  • Australian stone supplier guide, How to clean natural stone without damaging it. Read 16/11/2026.
  • Godfrey Hirst, Maintenance Recommendations for Commercial Sheet Vinyl, Australia / New Zealand (August 2022). Read 16/11/2026.
  • ACO Drain, Understanding slip resistance (secondary summary of AS 4586). Read 16/11/2026.
  • NSW EPA, Guidance for stormwater management: the drain is just for rain. Read 16/11/2026.

lessons.title: Resilient floors: strip, rinse, dry and recoat
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A council library in Hobart books a strip and recoat of a 150 m² reading room in sheet vinyl. The finish is yellowed and scuffed. A building manager says the floor was laid “years ago” and has no records. Staff will return in two days and children use the room.

The idea

Before a strip and recoat, ask what the floor is and when it was laid. An unrecorded older resilient floor cannot be ruled out as asbestos-containing by looking at it, so the Module 1 gate decides whether this job can start at all. If asbestos cannot be ruled out, stop and refer. This lesson applies only to floors confirmed asbestos-free in writing.

Read three sheets. The floor maker, the existing finish maker and the stripper maker can each limit the method. The approved setup record (Module 3) holds the product, the dilution, the dwell, the pad, the machine and the limits, all taken from those sheets. One maker’s sheet-vinyl guide is a useful example of the pattern: it lists dust removal, then a damp mop, then, where the site requires it, a stripping sequence. It is an example, not a rule for every floor.

Isolate. That guide says to cordon off the areas to be stripped and prohibit traffic until the work is completed. In the library, close the room, post signs and plan the return time with the building manager before the first mix.

The sequence, as one maker states it. Mix the stripping solution to the appropriate dilution and let it soak for the time its maker recommends. Machine scrub with a scrubbing pad; the guide names 300 rpm or lower for its own product, which is one maker’s example and not a setting to copy. Do not allow the stripping solution to dry on the floor. Remove the dirty solution with a wet vacuum or mop. Rinse the entire floor with fresh clean water, remove the rinse water and let the floor dry completely.

Check, then recoat. Verify residue removal by the finish maker’s own method and record the result before any coat goes on. Coat only a fully dry floor in thin, even coats, and give the return-to-use time the finish maker states. Collect wastewater and send it to the approved route: nothing but clean rainwater goes to the stormwater drain (Module 4). Post wet floor signs for as long as the floor is slippery, and tell staff how to report a spill.

When the saving matters. For routine maintenance the same guide says auto scrubbing in unobstructed areas takes approximately 20% of the time damp mopping does. A scrub-and-recoat is often the better offer than a full strip, but only the maker’s sheet and a test panel show whether the existing finish can take it.

See it

Strip and recoat on a confirmed asbestos-free resilient floor. Asbestos not ruled out means stop and refer first.

Do it in metric

The reading room is 150 m². A label states (an illustrative figure) 10 m² per litre of mixed solution, so the job needs 150 ÷ 10 = 15 L of mixed solution. At a label dilution of 1 part concentrate to 4 parts water, the 15 L splits into 15 ÷ 5 = 3 L concentrate and 12 L water.

A damp mop of the same room is estimated at 100 minutes. If auto scrubbing takes 20% of that, as one maker’s guide states for its own sites, the scrub is about 100 × 0.2 = 20 minutes. Quote from a timed test panel, not from the maker’s ratio.

Field download

The Resilient and timber job record has the gate questions, the three-maker lines, the dwell and rinse log, the residue-verification record and the return-to-use time.

Check yourself

The Module 5 check asks you to say when a resilient floor is a stop, order the sequence and name what to record before recoating.

Takeaway

Confirm asbestos-free first, take the method from the makers, never let the solution dry, rinse and dry fully, verify and record before recoating. Next: coated timber floors.

Sources for this lesson

  • Godfrey Hirst, Maintenance Recommendations for Commercial Sheet Vinyl, Australia / New Zealand (August 2022). Read 16/11/2026.
  • Safe Work Australia, Model Code of Practice: How to manage and control asbestos in the workplace. Read 16/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe New Zealand, Asbestos in Aotearoa New Zealand. Read 16/11/2026.

lessons.title: Coated timber floors: damp-only care and referral
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A homeowner in Perth asks for “the full works” on a coated timber floor. She has been using a steam mop every week. The coating looks cloudy near the kitchen, and there is a bare patch in front of the sink where the boards look grey.

The idea

Most timber floors in homes and offices have a factory or site-applied coating, and the coating is what the cleaner is cleaning. Care therefore begins with identifying the coating and the maker’s cleaning regime, and ends with a damp, well-wrung pad. The Australasian Timber Flooring Association (ATFA) publishes a care sheet on which this lesson relies.

Identify. Ask what the coating is and when it was last coated. Look at the floor in raking light for wear, cloudiness and bare patches. ATFA advises using the cleaning regime specified by the floor coating manufacturer, or, where that is not known, test rubbing an isolated area to verify the cleaner is compatible with the coating. Record both.

Steam. ATFA states that steam mops can cause peeling of the finish, whitening and a cloudy finish, and advises that unless the timber flooring or finish manufacturer says it is OK, it is safest to assume steam cleaning is not appropriate on a timber floor. The cloudy patch near the kitchen is consistent with that warning, but it is not proof. Say that, and offer to look.

Damp, not wet. ATFA advises damp mopping with a neutral pH wood floor cleaner or the product the finish manufacturer recommends, avoids harsh detergents and abrasive cleaners, and says the mop should be wrung out until it is moist before mopping. Use as little water as the job allows, wipe the edges, and remove spills at once. A dry or lightly damp pad for the final pass leaves no standing water.

Refer. Cleaning cannot put back a coating that has worn through. Photograph the grey patch with a scale, write down what you saw and tell the homeowner that a timber floor finisher should look at it. Do not apply a coat to try to hide wear unless the finish maker and a finisher have said it is suitable, and do not promise a result that cleaning cannot deliver.

See it

Coated timber floors. Identify, test, damp-mop and refer worn coating. Steam is not assumed safe.

Do it in metric

The room is 4.2 m × 6.0 m = 25.2 m². A bucket of 5 L at an illustrative label dilution of 1 part in 50 holds 5 ÷ 50 = 0.1 L, or 100 mL of cleaner. Two bucket fills cover the room if the mop is kept moist, not wet, and the water is changed when it greys.

Photograph the grey patch next to a 300 mm rule so a finisher can judge the size: a patch 0.6 m wide and 0.3 m deep is about 0.18 m² of the 25.2 m², which is under 1% of the floor.

Field download

The Resilient and timber job record also holds the timber coating check, the test-rub record, the damp-mop log and the referral note for a finisher.

Check yourself

The Module 5 check asks you to say what ATFA advises on steam, how wet the pad may be and when to refer a worn coating.

Takeaway

Identify the coating, test, damp-mop with a well-wrung pad, keep steam off unless the maker allows it, and refer worn coating to a finisher. Next: quoting, handover and the practical day.

Sources for this lesson

  • Australasian Timber Flooring Association, Floor care and maintenance (2016, hosted by Resene). Read 16/11/2026.
  • Godfrey Hirst, Maintenance Recommendations for Commercial Sheet Vinyl, Australia / New Zealand (August 2022). Read 16/11/2026.

modules.title: Module 6: Quoting, Handover and the Practical Day

lessons.title: Quoting: residential and commercial programs
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A property manager in Brisbane asks for a price to look after a 120 m² medical centre waiting room and corridor in sheet vinyl. The floor has been recoated twice and is dull. She wants a firm price this week, with GST, and a plan for the next year so there are no surprises.

The idea

A good quote makes the method, the scope and the limits visible. It starts with what the earlier modules produced: the pre-job check, the floor identification, the approved setup record and a timed test panel. Without them, a price is a guess.

Quote both ways. For a coated resilient floor, offer a full strip and recoat and a scrub and recoat. Say what each does and what each leaves behind. A scrub and recoat suits a floor whose finish is in sound condition; a full strip suits a floor with heavy build-up or a coating the maker says must go. The maker’s sheet and a test panel decide which one is offered, not the price. One maker’s guide states that auto scrubbing in unobstructed areas takes approximately 20% of the time of damp mopping, so the time saved is real, but it applies to that maker’s own sites.

Add GST correctly. A quote shows the price before GST, the GST and the total. The rate that applies is set by the country: 10% in Australia and 15% in New Zealand. Confirm the rate with your accountant, because the course does not give tax advice.

Programs. A residential job is usually a visit. A commercial site is better served by a program: a scheduled series of visits with set tasks, access hours and records. State the scope of each visit, who signs, what is excluded and how the next service date is set. Set that date from the maker’s sheet and measured wear, not a fixed number. For timber, ATFA advises using the cleaning regime specified by the coating maker or test rubbing an isolated area, so the program must include that check.

State the stops. Write the asbestos gate, the grout stop rule and the unknown-coating rule into the quote as conditions. A quote that says it assumes a documented asbestos-free floor protects the client and the contractor.

See it

Quoting. Both methods priced with GST, a program for commercial sites and the stops written in as conditions.

Do it in metric

The waiting room and corridor measure 120 m². At an illustrative A$14 per m² a full strip and recoat is 120 × 14 = A$1,680 before GST. With 10% GST that is 1,680 × 1.1 = A$1,848.

A scrub and recoat at an illustrative A$6 per m² is 120 × 6 = A$720 before GST, or A$792 with GST. The difference between the two offers, with GST, is 1,848 − 792 = A$1,056. The rates are invented for the example; price from your own costs and a timed test panel.

Field download

The Quote and program sheet has the both-ways price table with GST, the visit scope, the conditions and stops, and the next service date line.

Check yourself

The Module 6 final exam covers every module. This lesson adds quoting, GST and the program.

Takeaway

Price both methods with GST, from your own costs and a timed test panel, and write the stops in as conditions. Next: handover, records and the practical day.

Sources for this lesson

  • Godfrey Hirst, Maintenance Recommendations for Commercial Sheet Vinyl, Australia / New Zealand (August 2022). Read 16/11/2026.
  • Australasian Timber Flooring Association, Floor care and maintenance (2016, hosted by Resene). Read 16/11/2026.

lessons.title: Handover, records and the supervised practical day
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification in the evidence ledger.

On the job

Three hours after the last coat in a Newcastle medical centre, the property manager wants to unlock the doors. A cleaner is mopping the corridor. A client asks, “When can staff walk on it, and what should happen next time?” The crew has photos, but nothing is written down.

The idea

The job is not finished until the next person can use the floor safely and the records can answer a question a year later. Handover is therefore a short, written, repeatable step.

Before leaving. Check the floor in raking light. Check that the floor is dry and that the signs and barriers are still in place. One maker’s guide says to post wet floor signs for spillages; the same applies after a clean. Take after photos from the same positions as the before photos. Give the property manager the return-to-use time that the finish maker states, not one you invented.

The handover page. A single page holds the floor identified, the product and dilution used, the approved setup lines, the photos, the return-to-use time, the care sheet and the next service date. Add what you did not do and why: for example, a worn patch referred to a finisher, or a grout line left alone because it was loose. Keep a copy.

Records. Keep the pre-job sheet, the approved setup record, the job record and the handover page together. For timber, include the test-rub result. Keep records as long as the client contract and the insurer require, and check the period locally. Waste goes to the approved route, never to the stormwater drain: nothing other than clean rainwater should enter it.

The supervised practical day. The online part builds judgement. The practical day shows skill. An assessor watches you complete the pre-job check, read an SDS, identify the floors, mix at the label dilution, record the approved setup, run the pre-start check, test the grout, clean a panel, identify a timber coating and write the handover. All work is on documented panels and boards. Any scenario that suggests suspected asbestos ends with stop and refer. The assessor records Met or Not yet; critical criteria must all be met.

See it

Handover, records and the practical day. Signs stay up, the maker's return-to-use time is given and records are kept.

Do it in metric

Take three photos per site: the whole room, the worst area and the edge at the door. For 6 sites that is 3 × 6 = 18 photos and 6 one-page records, each with the date, the room in square metres and the return-to-use time.

Record the floor area on the handover page, for example 120 m², and the number of bucket changes. A page that carries real numbers answers the question a year later.

Field download

The Quote and program sheet also holds the handover page, the records checklist and the practical-day preparation list.

Check yourself

The final exam now covers the whole course. It has 20 questions and an 80% pass mark.

Takeaway

Check, photograph, state the maker's return-to-use time, write the one-page handover and keep the records. The practical day proves the skills on documented panels. Next: the final exam.

Sources for this lesson

  • Australasian Timber Flooring Association, Floor care and maintenance (2016, hosted by Resene). Read 16/11/2026.
  • NSW EPA, Guidance for stormwater management: the drain is just for rain. Read 16/11/2026.
